chief_complaint: shortness of breath and chest tightness during exercise in young athlete
hpi_details: An 18-year-old female athlete presents with shortness of breath and chest tightness during exercise. The symptoms occur with exertion and have become more frequent.
ideas: She thinks she has simply fallen out of shape after her training break or that breathing cold morning air during track practice is irritating her lungs.
concerns: She is worried that she will lose her varsity spot and her college athletic scholarship if she cannot finish her upcoming races.
expectations: She hopes to be prescribed an inhaler today so she can breathe clearly and be ready for next week's qualifying meet.

investigation_events.title: Exercise challenge spirometry
investigation_events.availability_message: The exercise challenge spirometry result is now available.

results.value: 16% fall from baseline at 10 minutes, returning toward baseline after salbutamol

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Exercise-Induced Bronchospasm is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Diagnosis is supported by variable airflow limitation demonstrated with spirometry and, when necessary, an exercise or bronchoprovocation challenge; cardiac evaluation is reserved for concerning exertional symptoms or abnormal cardiac findings.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: shortness of breath and chest tightness during exercise in young athlete
Key HPI features: An 18-year-old female athlete presents with shortness of breath and chest tightness during exercise that have become more frequent.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Exercise-Induced Bronchospasm.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Exercise-Induced Bronchospasm.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Exertional angina without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Chest pain with exertion in an older or high-risk patient must still exclude ischaemia.
management_principles: Perform spirometry and, when needed, exercise or bronchoprovocation testing; assess cardiac red flags and obtain cardiac evaluation when indicated
Use a short-acting bronchodilator before exercise when appropriate and reassess if symptoms persist
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Exercise-Induced Bronchospasm
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Exercise-Induced Bronchospasm

Implement evidence-based management plan: Confirm variable airflow limitation with spirometry or provocation testing, assess cardiac red flags, and use a short-acting bronchodilator before exercise when appropriate

teaching.one_liner: Airways narrow a few minutes into exercise, so chest tightness and breathlessness peak after stopping — not a cardiac pattern.
red_flags: Chest pain with exertion in an older or high-risk patient must still exclude ischaemia

must_ask.say: Does it start a few minutes into exercise, or after you stop?
Do you wheeze or cough with it?
Is it worse in cold air, or at a particular time of year?
Do you have asthma, eczema, or hay fever, in you or your family?
Have you used an inhaler, and did it help?
Any chest pain radiating to your arm, or fainting?

history.answer: I've been getting short of breath and feeling tightness in my chest whenever I exercise, and it's happening more frequently lately.
It started about two months ago during track practice. At first it happened only occasionally, but now it occurs almost every time I run hard.
It usually kicks in about ten to fifteen minutes into intense running, or right after I finish a hard workout, and takes about twenty to thirty minutes to settle down.
Normal daily walking or climbing stairs is completely fine. It only happens when I push myself into high-intensity running or track workouts.
It comes in distinct episodes tied to strenuous workouts. Once I rest for half an hour, my breathing returns completely to normal.
Yes, I hear a faint high-pitched whistling sound when I breathe out during those episodes.
I get a dry hacky cough after hard workouts when my chest feels tight, but I don't bring up any phlegm.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or night sweats.
It feels like a band squeezing across my chest when I run hard, but it's not a crushing center-of-the-chest pressure and it doesn't shoot anywhere else.
It is definitely worse when I train outside in cold, dry winter air, or on high pollen days in the spring.
No, I sleep comfortably on a single flat pillow and I never wake up gasping or coughing at night.
No racing heartbeats out of proportion, no lightheadedness, and I have never passed out.
No, I have never coughed up any blood.
No swelling in my feet or legs, and my weight has remained completely steady.
No pain or swelling in either calf, no recent long flights or surgeries, and I don't take any hormone medications.
No unusual fatigue, my periods aren't heavy, and I have never noticed dark or tarry stools.
No tingling around my lips or in my fingers, and it doesn't feel like panic or anxiety—it strictly happens with physical exertion.
I had seasonal sneezing and runny nose in the spring when I was younger, but I've never been diagnosed with asthma or eczema.
I have never used an inhaler because I never had breathing trouble like this before two months ago.
I have always been healthy and have no history of chronic heart, lung, or metabolic disease.
I have never had any surgeries and I've never been admitted to a hospital.
I don't take any prescription medicines, over-the-counter drugs, or health supplements.
No, I don't take beta blockers, aspirin, ibuprofen, or any other pain relievers.
I don't have any known allergies to medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes, vaped, or used any tobacco products.
I only drink an occasional beer at social gatherings once or twice a month, and nothing more.
I am an eighteen-year-old student and collegiate track athlete, living on campus in a dorm.
No exposure to chemical fumes, industrial dust, mold, birds, or secondhand smoke.
My mother has mild asthma and pollen allergies, but no one in my family has had early heart attacks or sudden unexpected cardiac death.
My last period was two weeks ago, my cycles are regular every 28 days, I am not sexually active, and there is no chance of pregnancy.
I thought maybe I just lost my stamina after taking a break, or that breathing in the cold morning air during track drills was irritating my lungs.
I'm terrified that I'll lose my spot on the varsity team and my college scholarship if I keep having to stop during races.
I'm hoping you can give me an inhaler today so my chest opens up and I can run in my qualifying meet next week.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 116/74 mmHg, heart rate 68 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, athletic young woman in no acute distress; no accessory muscle use, lip cyanosis, or digital clubbing.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor; sclerae are non-icteric.
Nasal mucosa mildly boggy with pale swelling; posterior pharynx clear without erythema or tonsillar enlargement.
Normal jugular venous pressure without distention.
Symmetric chest expansion with normal tactile fremitus and no chest wall tenderness.
Resonant percussion notes throughout all lung zones bilaterally.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally at rest with normal vesicular breathing and no wheezing, rhonchi, or crackles.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, clicks, or friction rubs.
No pitting edema in bilateral lower extremities.
Both calves are soft, symmetric, non-tender, and without cords, erythema, or warmth.
